event.title: Book Talk: Nuremberg's Citizen Prosecutor
event.description:
Join the Center for Human Rights and International Justice as Professor Gregory Gordon presents his new book, which chronicles the remarkable life of Benjamin Ferencz. Ferencz is known as one of the twentieth century’s great warriors for justice, from Nuremberg to the first trial of the International Criminal Court. 

This event is co-sponosred with the Stanford University Libraries.

About the author: 

Gregory S. Gordon is a Professor of Law at Peking University School of Transnational Law. Not long after earning undergraduate and law degrees from Berkeley, he served as an attorney at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda on the landmark “Media” cases, the first international post-Nuremberg incitement prosecutions of media executives, earning a commendation from U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno. He subsequently worked with the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), serving, in sequence, as a street crime, white collar crime, organized crime and then human rights prosecutor (the latter for the Office of Special Investigations, the so-called “Nazi Hunters Unit”). He has tried 24 cases, 23 to a favorable verdict. Professor Gordon was detailed by DOJ to Sierra Leone to conduct a post-civil war justice assessment and served as a Special Assistant U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia. From 2006 to 2014, he was a professor at UND Law and served as Professor Gordon is the author of Atrocity Speech Law: Foundation, Fragmentation, Fruition (Oxford University Press, 2017) and his new monograph Nuremberg’s Citizen Prosecutor: Benjamin Ferencz and the Birth of International Justice, was published by the University of Virginia Press in November 2025. He is pursuing a PhD at Stockholm University Faculty of Law proposing fixes to a broken atrocity victim justice framework based on the doctrinal and procedural innovations developed by Ben Ferencz during his career. Since 2023, Professor Gordon has served as an advisor to Ukrainian prosecutors related to Russian war crimes arising from the invasion of Ukraine. In 2025, he was chosen to receive the “World of Upstanders Award” by the NGO World Without Genocide, in recognition of his life’s work on behalf of protecting victims of gross human rights violations.

event.title: ESE Seminar - Ruben Juanes: "Photoporomechanics: Towards stress-tensor tomography in 3D granular media"
event.description:
Abstract

Ruben Juanes (joint work with Wei Li, Yue Meng, Shiyao Wang)

Photoporomechanics: Towards stress-tensor tomography in 3D granular mediaRuben Juanes (joint work with Wei Li, Yue Meng, Shiyao Wang)At a fundamental level, the macroscopic response of granular media depends on the spatial organization of contact forces between grains—the so-called force chains. Despite their critical importance, force chains in granular media have been characterized and analyzed almost exclusively in 2D systems. To address this knowledge gap, we recently developed a new approach: a tomographic imaging technique (interference optical projection tomography, or IOPT), which by combining the principles of photoelasticity and tomography, provides direct visualization of the particles’ force network, thus circumventing the need of constitutive models of particle-particle contact (Li and Juanes, 2024). With our novel experimental technique, we provide the microscopic explanation for why a pack of angular particles is stronger than one of round particles: they form interconnected force networks that are less likely to buckle when under stress than the isolated chains in a pack of round particles.While early results show the potential of our approach, currently this new technique is limited to reconstructing the 3D scalar field of stress-anisotropy under axisymmetric stressconditions, for example, triaxial shear. Here, we present the reconstruction of the grain-scale full tensor field in 3D (stress-tensor tomography) and focus on the study of the 3D internal stresses in a single particle subject to arbitrary loading conditions. If time permits, we will present early results extending the experimentation, modeling, and inversion of the stress field from the single-particle scale to the ensemble-scale of 3D granular packs. The ability to interrogate the grain-scale stresses in granular media will enable new understanding of granular media and help predict the behavior of fluid-coupled granular media in landslides, liquefaction, and earthquakes.

Bio

Ruben Juanes is professor in Civil and Environmental Engineering, and Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences at MIT, where he has been since 2006. He is an expert in fluid flow through porous media and in geomechanics, and has applied his research to the fields of energy resources, carbon capture and storage, gas hydrates, water infiltration and soil irrigation, and induced seismicity. He holds an undergraduate degree from University of A Coruña (Spain) and graduate degrees from UC Berkeley, all in Civil and Environmental Engineering. He is a fellow of the American Geophysical Union and the American Physical Society.

References

Li, W., & Juanes, R. (2024). Dynamic imaging of force chains in 3D granular media. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 121(14), e2319160121.

event.title: International Education Week: Scholar Research Presentation with Iryna Barba
event.description:
In celebration of International Education Week, we are hosting scholar presentations about their research. Join us for a talk by Iryna Barba, Associate Professor at the State University of Intelligent Technologies and Telecommunications (Ukraine) and Fulbright Visiting Scholar at Stanford University.

Her presentation, “Advanced Transmission Technologies for Fixed Broadband Access Networks: A Global and Ukrainian Perspective,” explores how to deliver multi-gigabit internet over existing copper infrastructure without costly full re-cabling. Fixed broadband remains critical for reliable, low-latency connectivity, especially in emergencies and wartime conditions, and for closing the digital divide in rural and underserved communities.

The presentation is open to students, researchers, and anyone interested in telecommunications, digital inclusion, and international scholarly exchange.

Presenter:
Iryna Barba, Associate Professor, State University of Intelligent Technologies and Telecommunications (Ukraine); Fulbright Visiting Scholar, Stanford University

event.title: Know Before You Decide to Go: Understanding the Risks When Considering International Experiences
event.description:
This workshop introduces Stanford’s International Travel Risk Assessment, a quick, personalized, process that helps travelers understand the health, safety, and security risks of a proposed travel destination. We’ll cover how Stanford’s International Travel Policy works and you’ll learn where to find reliable ratings/advisories, how to request  tailored guidance, and how to identify top risks. The session is designed to help you think through physical and mental health needs, identity and cultural considerations, and local events that might affect your trip. You’ll leave knowing whether your destination is permitted (for undergraduates), what challenges to prepare for, what emergency resources are available, and who to contact with questions.

BONUS: If you're planning to find an internship abroad, in the second half of the session, we'll review the tools for vetting an international internship host from a health, safety, and security perspective.

Jillian Schwedler — Are the Streets Still Talking? Protests and Evolving Repression in the Middle East
event.description:
Although the Middle East/SWANA region encompasses a diverse range of authoritarian regimes, protests are surprisingly common across much of it. Mass mobilizations such as the Arab uprisings and Iran’s Woman, Life, Freedom movement attract international attention, yet less is known about the thousands of smaller protests that precede and follow them. This talk will examine patterns of protest across the region and explore how repression is changing in the age of mass surveillance and artificial intelligence.

This event is co-sponsored by CDDRL's Program on Arab Reform and Development and the Middle Eastern Studies Forum.

ABOUT THE SPEAKER

Jillian Schwedler is Distinguished Professor of Political Science at the City University of New York’s Hunter College and the Graduate Center and Nonresident Senior Fellow at the Crown Center for the Middle East at Brandeis University. She has served in elected leadership positions for the American Political Science Association and the Middle East Studies Association. She has been a member of the Editorial Committee of the International Journal of Middle East Studies and is currently Chair of the Editorial Committee for the Middle East Research and Information Project (MERIP), publishers of Middle East Report.

Prof. Schwedler’s books include the award-winning Faith in Moderation: Islamist Parties in Jordan and Yemen (2006), Policing and Prisons in the Middle East (with Laleh Khalili, 2010), and The Political Science of the Middle East (with Marc Lynch and Sean Yom, 2022).  Her articles have appeared in numerous journals, including World Politics, Comparative Politics, Contention, and Social Movement Studies.  Her most recent book, Protesting Jordan: Geographies of Power and Dissent (2022) was recipient of best book awards from the National Endowment for Democracy and the Middle East Institute.

event.title: Race and Gender in the Global Hispanophone: Bound Brothers Chinese Labor, Masculinity, and Nation in Nineteenth-Century Peru and Chile
event.address: 450 Jane Stanford Way, Building 260, Stanford, CA 94305
event.description:
The Race and Gender in the Global Hispanophone Research Group is excited to invite you to a talk by Professor Heidi Tinsman (Professor of History at UC Irvine) on her forthcoming book, Bound Brothers: Chinese Labor, Masculinity, and Nation in Nineteenth-Century Peru and Chile. The talk will be on Monday, November 16th from 4:00pm to 5:30pm in Pigott Hall, Room 252. 

RSVP HERE FOR RACE AND GENDER IN THE GLOBAL HISPANOPHONE EVENT

Abstract: 

Bound Brothers asks how Peruvian and Chilean nations were shaped by connections to China and the labor and agency of Chinese people within South America. Indentured Chinese workers brought through the so-called “coolie trade” was vital to the capitalist export economies that anchored South American republics and fueled armed conflict between Peru and Chile during the War of the Pacific (1879-1883). This book highlights the significance of gender, especially masculinity, to the politics of Chinese labor and nation-making in Peru and Chile. Men comprised ninety-nine percent of Chinese people in nineteenth-century Peru and Chile. Why and how did this matter? The book traces Chinese men’s everyday connections to each other as well as to Chilean and Peruvian men. The term bound brothers refers to fraternal solidarity among men as well as to Chinese bondage as indentured contract workers. Chinese men recreated all-male associations common in China to negotiate life in Peru and Chile. Chinese sworn brotherhoods, merchant guilds, and mutual-aid societies organized the collective defense of Chinese interests and asserted control over Chinese labor and commerce. Chinese religious ceremonies cemented loyalties between men and commitments to common cause. In many instances, bonds between men were forged through ties to women. Chinese men created shared patrilineal families by marrying related wives; they claimed other men as brothers through Catholic godparenting and baptism. Male solidarity was integral to Chinese forms of Peruvian and Chilean belonging.

Speaker bio:

Heidi Tinsman is a Professor of History at the University of California, Irvine, where she also currently directs the Center for Latin American & Caribbean Studies. Her research focuses on gender and labor in modern Latin America and the Americas, with a particular emphasis on feminist materialist paradigms in transnational history. Professor Tinsman is the author of Partners in Conflict: The Politics of Gender, Sexuality, and Labor in the Chilean Agrarian Reform, 1950-1973 (Duke University Press, 2002) and Buying into the Regime: Consumption and Grapes in Cold War Chile and the United States (Duke University Press, 2014). She is also the co-editor of Imagining Our Americas: Toward a Transnational Frame with Sandhya Shukla (Duke University Press, 2007). Her current book project, Bound Brothers: Chinese Labor, Masculinity and Nation in Nineteenth-Century Peru and Chile, is forthcoming with University of California Press. Her work has been awarded numerous accolades including the John Simon Memorial Guggenheim Fellowship, a Fulbright-Hays Faculty Research Fellowship, and a Fellowship from the American Council of Learned Societies.

event.title: Stanford Energy Seminar | Electrified metamaterial reactors for process intensified thermochemistry | Jonathan Fan, Stanford University
event.description:
The electrification of thermochemical processes with clean electricity has great potential as both an immediate and long-term solution towards the scalable decarbonization of chemical production. In this talk, I will discuss new paradigms in electrified thermochemical reactors based on high frequency electromagnetic fields. I will first discuss metamaterial reactors in which a volumetric open-cell lattice baffle is inductively heated with heating profiles tailored by reaction engineering considerations. I will next discuss resonant metamaterial reactors, a new class of reactor in which energy transduction is achieved by principles in resonant wireless power transfer. I will finally discuss how high frequency electric fields can be coupled to feedstocks and catalysts to facilitate new modes of selective energy transfer.

Jonathan Fan is an Associate Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering at Stanford University, where he is researching topics at the intersection of electromagnetics, optics, and sustainability. He received his bachelor’s degree with highest honors from Princeton University and his doctorate from Harvard University. He is the recipient of the Air Force Young Investigator Award, Sloan Foundation Fellowship in Physics, Packard Foundation Fellowship, and the Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers. He is a fellow of Optica.

Seminar Background

The Stanford Energy Seminar delivers a wide variety of perspectives on energy to the Stanford community, including academics, entrepreneurs, policymakers, and executives with utilities and non-profits. The series has been a mainstay of energy engagement at Stanford for nearly 20 years and is one of the flagship programs of the Precourt Institute for Energy. 
 

Anyone with an interest in energy is welcome to join! You can enjoy seminars in the following ways:

  • Attend live. The auditorium may change quarter by quarter, so check each seminar event to confirm the location. Explore the current quarter's schedule.
  • Watch live in a browser livestream if available. Check each seminar event for its unique livestream URL.
  • Watch recordings of past seminars 
    • Available on the Past Energy Seminars page and the Energy Seminars playlist of the Stanford Energy YouTube channel
  • (For students) Take the seminar as a 1-unit class (CEE 301/ENERGY 301/MS&E 494)

event.title: An Extreme Event: 🌿 Community-Led Social Innovation in Times of Crisis in Nepal
event.location: Stanford Graduate School of Business, 643 Jane Stanford Way, Stanford, CA. 94305
event.location_name: Stanford Graduate School of Business, 643 Jane Stanford Way, Stanford, CA. 94305
event.description:
About this Event

​When devastating floods recently swept through Nepal, the first line of defense wasn't distant aid organizations—it was local communities leveraging decades of grassroots social innovation. Grounded in trusted relationships, deep local knowledge, and community-owned infrastructure, local leaders and volunteers mobilized instantly to shelter displaced families, deliver urgent care, and close critical gaps that institutional relief often overlooks.

​What does this teach us about the grounded architecture of climate resilience, disaster response, and community-driven social impact?

​Effective crisis response and lasting social transformation depend not just on how fast emergency aid arrives, but on what equity-centered systems and relationships are already in place long before disaster strikes.

​Key Questions We Will Explore

  • ​Disaster Response & Local Infrastructure: How can community-owned spaces (like READ Centers) pivot seamlessly from daily learning hubs into critical emergency response centers during acute crises?

  • ​Localizing Power & Capital: How do we shift funding, decision-making, and resources to local leadership before disaster strikes to build genuine, long-term climate resilience?

  • ​Bridging Grassroots & Institutional Response: How can international humanitarian agencies and governments partner with local networks effectively without undermining community trust or agency?

  • ​Community Co-Design in Action: What does it practically look like to design with communities rather than for them when navigating high-stakes, unpredictable environments?

​What We’ll Explore

​Join Design for Extreme Affordability for an intimate, story-rich conversation with READ Global. Drawing on firsthand experiences from Nepal’s community-owned READ Centers, they will stories of extreme impact and share lessons from the field on:

  • ​🌾 Local Infrastructure for Social Impact: Leveraging community assets as engines for continuous social innovation.

  • ​🤝 Bridging Grassroots Innovation & Institutional Response: Fostering aligned, equity-centered disaster response.

  • ​🌍 Investing in Systems-Level Resilience: Reimagining climate adaptation through relational networks and localized governance.

​The presentation will be followed by an interactive Q&A and discussion.

​Bridging Grassroots & Institutional Response: How can international humanitarian agencies and governments partner with local networks effectively without undermining community trust or agency?

​Community Co-Design in Action: What does it practically look like to design with communities rather than for them when navigating high-stakes, unpredictable environments?

​What We’ll Explore

​Join Design for Extreme Affordability for an intimate, story-rich conversation with READ Global. Drawing on firsthand experiences from Nepal’s community-owned READ Centers, they will stories of extreme impact and share lessons from the field on:

​🌾 Local Infrastructure for Social Impact: Leveraging community assets as engines for continuous social innovation.

​🤝 Bridging Grassroots Innovation & Institutional Response: Fostering aligned, equity-centered disaster response.

​🌍 Investing in Systems-Level Resilience: Reimagining climate adaptation through relational networks and localized governance.

​The presentation will be followed by an interactive Q&A and discussion.

event.description:
The French and Italian Department and French Speaking Worlds: Here and Now present: A Book talk on D’abord ils sont venus chercher les mots [First They Came for Words], les Arènes, 2026, by Prof. Cécile Alduy, in conversation with Prof. Joshua Landy. 

An Author Caught Up by Her Subject
A professor of literature at Stanford and a discourse analysis scholar, Cécile Alduy has spent years analyzing how the far right wages its culture war. In 2022, in La Langue de Zemmour (Zemmour’s Language), she showed how the presidential candidate was distorting concepts and history to short-circuit rational thinking and appeal to hatred and fear. Then, on January 20, 2025, her research caught up with her brutally. At Stanford, her life and work were upended, like those of colleagues, students and workers in universities, schools, administrations, and scientific labs nationwide, when the new administration unleashed terror and censorship on culture and science. In this first-person account, she tells what the far right does once in power, day to day.

A New Linguistic and Political Regime
“Women,” “climate crisis,” “disability,” “diversity,” “Black,” “equality,” “gender,” “social justice,” “LGBT,” “prejudice,” “racism,” “vaccine” ... These words, among others, have been banned or blacklisted by the Trump administration since March 2025. Cécile Alduy conducts a gripping investigation into this list, which grew from a handful of demonized terms into over 480 flammable ones through anticipatory obedience, self-censorship, and overcompliance. She shows how the culture war has now given way to a real-world war against individuals. Meanwhile, the tech world has provided the tools to track down and eliminate words and lives alike. “Deportation” is no longer a term from history books: it is state policy.

Dystopia as Daily Life
The book is about the disappeared: the dead and the vanished words, forbidden names and identities, twisted meanings and drained values. It explains what this new political and linguistic regime is and does: how it seeks to control what can be said and thought, and bends reality to fit its ideological fictions.

How can we analyze a power that is destroying the very concepts we need to understand it? It is a question of survival: intellectual, and, for many, already physical. Cécile Alduy started writing out of fear and paralysis: inscribing these stories became progressively an act of resistance, a search for meaning in a world that has become senseless, and the first step toward reclaiming the right to a language that is just and whole. 

If this book retraces the grip that far-right language has on speech and on minds, in the United States but also already in France, it is, also, a manual for breaking free.

Cécile Alduy is a professor of literature at Stanford University and an associate scholar at Cevipof, Sciences Po Paris. She is the author of La Langue de Zemmour (Seuil, 2022) and Marine Le Pen prise aux mots (Marine Le Pen Caught in Words, Seuil, 2015).

event.title: Using AI to Listen, Learn, and Act on Community Feedback
event.description:
Meaningful change begins with listening. Evidence shows that when we genuinely understand people’s needs and act on what we hear, we make better decisions that lead to better outcomes. So how can AI help nonprofits and foundations listen to more people, synthesize large volumes of data, and respond more effectively? Join SSIR and Feedback Labs for a 90-minute interactive session exploring AI for feedback and listening at scale. 

Building on Feedback Labs’ research and experience, we’ll hear case studies from nonprofits and foundations that are using AI to accelerate and scale listening without losing the nuance, trust, and human connection that make listening meaningful. Participants will discuss what’s working, what’s not, and what responsible AI-enabled listening can look like in practice. Whether you’re already experimenting with AI for listening or just beginning to explore its potential, you’ll leave with practical ideas and questions to help you determine where AI can, and can’t, strengthen your organization’s feedback and listening practices.

Join this interactive 90-minute program led by Alexis Banks, Director of Learning and Operations at Feedback Labs, and Annie Grier, Director of Community and Equity at Feedback Labs.

You can expect to: 

  • Walk away with an understanding of how to think about effective and responsible AI use in the context of community listening.
  • Learn from peers who are using AI to accelerate, scale, and strengthen their feedback processes.
  • Identify strategies and tools to support your organization’s feedback collection, analysis, and course correction.

Who should attend:  
This program is designed for leaders, nonprofit professionals, and changemakers working to address complex social and organizational challenges.
This session is particularly valuable if you are:

  • Responsible for collecting, analyzing, or acting on feedback from communities, program participants, or grantees
  • Curious about how new tech tools may help your organization but concerned about preserving trust, accuracy, and quality in your listening practices
  • Experimenting with AI tools and looking to learn more from peers, compare approaches, and refine your practice

Register now to explore how AI can help your organization listen at scale, responsibly and with care.

 

Program Features:

Meet the Speakers

Alexis Banks (she/her) is the Director of Learning and Operations at Feedback Labs. Alexis designs and facilitates learning initiatives on high-quality constituent feedback and listening, such as the Feedback Crash Course and Listening in this Moment series. She also oversees the organization's coaching for nonprofits and foundations and feedback resources. Before Feedback Labs, Alexis worked with foundations, international organizations, and community groups to design and launch feedback loops and managed training and coaching for thousands of organizations around the world at GlobalGiving and Root Change. 

Annie Grier (she/her) is the Director of Community and Equity at Feedback Labs. She builds and supports the feedback community, developing partnerships, supporting feedback professionals, and exploring how feedback can advance social equity. A macro social worker, she has spent more than a decade working across nonprofits, universities, and criminal justice systems, leading equity initiatives, designing programs, and conducting research and evaluation. Annie teaches social work at Fordham and Columbia Universities and serves on the Special Commission to Advance Macro Practice in Social Work.

Guest Speakers

Mariel Beasley is Head of Product and Insights at SaverLife, leading the organization’s Research and Insights and Member Experience functions. Mariel blends rigorous research with practical strategies to design impactful, user-centric solutions that measurably enhance financial health and advance financial inclusion and equity. Throughout her career, Mariel’s passion for building a world where everyone can achieve financial security has guided her professional journey, including serving as a Peace Corps volunteer in the Dominican Republic, working for Boulder County Housing and Human Services, and, most recently, co-founding and directing the Common Cents Lab, a behavioral science research lab at Duke University.

Ayawa Fiagbedzi is Manager, Strategic Learning & Impact at The Rockefeller Foundation, where she helps shape how the Foundation uses evidence to drive strategy, improve performance, and deepen impact. With experience spanning philanthropy, government, and global development, she brings a systems-level perspective to embedding evidence into decision-making and building organizational learning capacity.

  Interactive Sessions: Participants will be able to ask questions and engage with the presenters and other participants.

●      access to join the 90-minute live webinar program

●      on-demand webinar recording access for 12 months

●      downloadable slides

●      recommended resources

event.title: Authoritarian Markets: The Politics of China’s Banking Explosion
event.description:
Conventional wisdom holds that banking markets flourish where property rights are secure, the rule of law is strong, and the state keeps its hands off. China has none of these. Yet over the past three decades, the number of Chinese banks grew exponentially, and competition became fierce. Why? In Authoritarian Markets: The Politics of China’s Banking Explosion (Cornell University Press, 2026), Adam Y. Liu argues that China’s banking market grew not despite authoritarian rule but because of it. The banking sector, he argues, is a market of the state, by the state, and for the state. Drawing on a decade of fieldwork and an extensive array of original data, Liu uncovers the political logic of banking market development in China and authoritarian states more broadly and explores what this means for the future of China’s economy.

Speaker: Adam Y. Liu is an Assistant Professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, National University of Singapore. His research focuses on Chinese politics and political economy. He earned his PhD from Stanford University, where his dissertation on the politics of China's banking development won the 2020 BRICS Economic Research Award.

event.title: Earth & Planetary Sciences Seminar - Prof. Peng Ni "Unraveling Earth’s dynamic history through sublithospheric diamonds"
event.address: 450 Jane Stanford Way, Building 320, Stanford, CA 94305
event.description:
Abstract: Most natural diamonds form at depths of 120 to 200 km in Earth’s lithospheric mantle. A small fraction, however, originates much deeper. This group of diamonds, known as sublithospheric diamonds, includes some of the largest and finest diamonds in the world. These diamonds can contain mineral inclusions that represent some of the deepest samples of Earth’s interior. In this talk, I will show how the chemistry of these inclusions records the geological history experienced by their host diamonds, providing a unique window into the dynamic processes that have shaped our planet over time.

Speaker Bio: Peng Ni is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Earth, Planetary, and Space Sciences at the University of California, Los Angeles. His research focuses on understanding the large-scale geochemical processes that have shaped Earth, Moon, and other terrestrial bodies throughout their formation, differentiation, and evolution. His group combines a wide range of approaches, including non-traditional stable isotope geochemistry, high-pressure high-temperature experiments, studies of natural sample studies, and geochemical modeling. His recent work includes investigating the recycling of surface materials into Earth’s deep interior using diamond inclusions; studying Apollo samples to better understand the Moon’s volatile budget and volcanic activity; and experimentally constraining the behavior of moderately volatile elements during evaporation processes.

event.title: German Studies Lecture Series: Jutta Eming - How Do You Dance a Cabinet of Curiosities?
event.address: 450 Jane Stanford Way, Building 260, Stanford, CA 94305
event.description:
Please join German Studies Lecture Series for How Do You Dance a Cabinet of Curiosities? A conversation with Professor Jutta Eming (Freie Universität Berlin).

As a collection and exhibition convention, a Cabinet of Curiosity or Wunderkammer is regarded as a historical intermediate stage between the medieval treasury and the modern museum. It was widespread throughout Europe from the 16th to 18th century until its holdings began to be distributed to newly founded natural history, art, or ethnological museums in the 18th and 19th century. Taking a recent choreography as a starting point, this talk introduces the view that the Wunderkammer is not primarily an early modern form of collection, but a cultural-historical phenomenon that spans epochs and is part of a continuum of discourses on the marvelous. This includes the fact that the Wunderkammer has obviously become a broader cultural studies topic and forms a reference for a variety of recent academic and non-academic trends. In premodern times these cabinets constitute a European view of the world with curiosity in “monstrous” races on its margins, and a practice of perception in which narration, appropriation, collecting, and presentation are closely linked. In recent times this interest in curiosity has flipped in emancipatory ways: The Wunderkammer now seems to provide a space in which humans negotiate the limits of binary identity and redefine their place in the world.

event.title: How New is the New Nuclear Age?
event.description:
About the event: Since the mid-2010s, scholars and analysts have declared the emergence of a dangerous ‘new’ or ‘third’ nuclear age. Beyond academia, the concept of the new nuclear age is proving influential with policymakers in a range of countries. The new nuclear age is understood to be characterized by technological change, nuclear multipolarity, eroding constraints on the behavior and competition of nuclear-armed states, and the likely emergence of new nuclear powers. That said, it remains unclear how we should understand the new nuclear age in broader terms: how new is it and does it require new theoretical frameworks to understand? Bell subjects the concept of the new nuclear age to scrutiny. He connects the discussion of the new nuclear age to ongoing but mostly separate debates about nuclear history and the ‘Theory of the Nuclear Revolution’ (TNR). The increasing body of literature challenging TNR reveals a more competitive, complex, and dangerous nuclear past than our prior understandings, but in doing so, it draws attention to continuities between the past and the emerging nuclear age. Bell then examines the empirical features thought to define the new nuclear age and show that many have historical precedent and do not require novel theoretical frameworks to understand. The new nuclear age may, therefore, be somewhat less new, though perhaps no less dangerous, than it appears.

About the speaker: Mark Bell is an Associate Professor of Political Science at the University of Minnesota. His book, Nuclear Reactions: How Nuclear-Armed States Behave, won the ISA Foreign Policy Analysis Section's best book award. Other work has been published in International Organization, International Security, International Studies Quarterly, Journal of Conflict Resolution, Journal of Strategic Studies, and Texas National Security Review. Policy-oriented work has been published in Foreign Affairs, War on the Rocks, and The Washington Quarterly. He holds a Ph.D from MIT, a Master's in Public Policy from Harvard Kennedy School, and a B.A. from St Anne’s College, Oxford University.

event.title: Smart Strategies for Holiday Eating
event.description:
The winter holiday season is almost here. This time of year, we may look forward to joyful experiences and time spent with loved ones. Yet, many of us also anticipate what can feel like the inevitable accompaniment to all these good times: too much food, drinks, sweets, and the resulting unhealthy yo-yo weight cycling.

How can we set ourselves up for a healthy holiday season? One where we gain joy and memories, but not weight? Join us for this noontime webinar to learn how to "maintain, not gain" during the 2026 holiday season.

We will discuss how to successfully navigate holiday dinners and buffets, how to apply the hunger/fullness scale to prevent overeating, and how to practice mindful eating to be intentional about food choices. You will also learn how to make healthy versions of your favorite holiday treats.

This class will be recorded and a one-week link to the recording will be shared with all registered participants.

To receive incentive points, attend at least 80% of the live session or listen to the entire recording within one week.

event.title: The Dangers of Focusing on the Danger of Digital Media Use
event.room_number: Studio S40 - bring your Stanford ID card/mobile ID to enter the building
event.description:
Join the Tech Impact and Policy Center on November 17th from 12PM–1PM Pacific for a seminar with Robin Nabi.

Stanford affiliates are invited to join us at 11:40 AM for lunch, prior to the seminar.  The Fall Seminar Series continues through December; see our Fall Seminar Series page for speakers and topics. Sign up for our newsletter for announcements. 

About the Seminar:

Extensive attention has been paid to the potential harms of media consumption generally, and social media use in particular, with relatively little consideration given to the potential psychological benefits of media use. This talk will address why this bias exists and its potential for unintended negative consequences. Evidence of how self-selected and prescribed digital media content can support desirable outcomes, including reduced stress and procrastination, increased goal motivation and pursuit, and increased empathy and relational satisfaction, will be shared to highlight the need for better understanding of how to empower users to make media choices that can support their psychological well-being.

About the Speaker:

Robin L. Nabi is a Professor of Communication at the University of California, Santa Barbara. With degrees from Harvard and the University of Pennsylvania, she has published over 100 journal articles and book chapters investigating the effects of media use on emotional experiences, decision-making, and well-being. She is the co-editor of two volumes: The SAGE Handbook of Media Processes and Effects and Emotions in the Digital World (Oxford University Press). She is a Fellow of the International Communication Association, and her research has been featured in numerous media outlets, including the New York Times, the Los Angeles Times, USA Today, NPR, CBC/Radio-Canada, and the Harvard Business Review.

event.title: Applied Physics/Physics Colloquium:Mikhail Lukin - "New frontier of Quantum Computing"
event.description:
A broad effort is currently underway to develop quantum computers that can outperform classical counterparts for certain computational, simulation or sensing tasks. The practical realization of such systems and exploration of their potential capabilities and limitations are central themes in the new field of quantum science and engineering. A central challenge in quantum computing is error suppression, which requires quantum error correction for large-scale processing. However, the overhead involved in creating error-corrected "logical" qubits-where information is redundantly encoded across multiple physical qubits-presents a significant obstacle to scalable quantum computing. In this talk, we will discuss recent advances in the programmable, coherent manipulation of quantum systems using neutral atom arrays excited into Rydberg states. These advances allow control over several hundred qubits and the exploration of quantum algorithms with encoded logical qubits and quantum error correction techniques. Enabled by the remarkable interdisciplinary effort, involving academia and industry, these advances have redefined the frontier of quantum computing and quantum information. They herald the advent of early error-corrected quantum computation, paving the way for new applications and inspiring a shift in addressing both the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead. Several examples of emerging applications, ranging from quantum many-body physics to quantum computing enhanced imaging will be discussed.
 

Dr. Mikhail Lukin is the Joshua and Beth Friedman University Professor of Physics at Harvard University, where he also serves as Co-Director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative. Dr. Lukin received his Ph.D. in physics from Texas A&M University. Dr. Lukin’s research focuses on quantum optics and quantum information science, with an emphasis on controlling strongly interacting atomic, optical, and solid-state systems. His work explores the quantum dynamics of many-body systems and develops novel applications in quantum computing, quantum simulation, quantum communication, and metrology. Dr. Lukin has pioneered advances in neutral atom quantum computing, quantum networking, and quantum sensing with both atomic and atom-like solid-state systems. Dr. Lukin has authored more than 540 scientific publications and is a member or fellow of the National Academy of Sciences, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Physical Society, and Optica. His honors include the Physics World Breakthrough of the Year (2024), Falling Walls Breakthrough of the Year in Physical Sciences (2023), the International Quantum Award (2022), the Norman F. Ramsey Prize of the American Physical Society (2022), the Charles Hard Townes Award of Optica (2021), the George Gamow Award (2020), and the Vannevar Bush Faculty Fellowship (2015). Earlier in his career, Dr. Lukin was recognized with the Alfred P. Sloan Fellowship, the Packard Fellowship for Science and Engineering, and the NSF CAREER Award. Today, Dr. Lukin continues to advance quantum information science through both research and leadership, helping shape the future of computing, communication, and measurement at the frontiers of physics.

event.title: Book Talk with Mikhail Fishman — The Successor: Boris Nemtsov, Vladimir Putin, and the Decline of Modern Russia
event.description:
When did Russia lose its chance of freedom? 1990: As a new openness sweeps Russia, a talented young physicist, Boris Nemtsov, begins his career in politics. Charismatic, confident, liberal and vehemently opposed to corruption, he swiftly rises to prominence. For the first time, another future seems possible. 2015: Putin holds the country in the grip of tyranny once more. Nemtsov, now his fiercest and most unrelenting opponent, is assassinated on a Moscow bridge. This is the story of how a nation's dreams of democracy died. Drawing on buried archives and off-the-record interviews, exiled journalist Mikhail Fishman gives a gripping insider account of the tragedy of modern Russia, told through many lives of Boris Nemtsov — activist, playboy, leader-in-waiting, dissident and, finally, victim. From the economic reforms under Boris Yeltsin to Vladimir Putin's oligarchy, through two wars in Chechnya and the invasion of Ukraine, this is the story of a man fired by the belief that Russia could, still, have another future.

SPEAKERS

Mikhail Fishman is one of Russia’s leading political journalists. Active since the late 1990s, he has chronicled Russia’s dramatic political life. He served as editor-in-chief of Russian Newsweek and The Moscow Times, as well as hosting the Friday night news round-up at independent news network TV Rain. In 2017, Fishman and Vera Krichevskaya released The Man Who Was Too Free, a documentary feature on Boris Nemtsov. It was the highest-grossing documentary in Russia in at least a decade and laid the groundwork for this book, which was an instant bestseller on Russian publication in 2022. Fishman faced increasing intimidation and suppression from the state; when Putin launched the invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he left for Amsterdam, where he now lives in exile with his family.

Kathryn Stoner is the Mosbacher Director of the Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL) and the Satre Family Senior Fellow at the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies (FSI). From 2017 to 2021, she served as FSI's Deputy Director. She is Professor of Political Science (by courtesy) at Stanford and teaches in the Department of Political Science, the Program on International Relations, and the Ford Dorsey Master's in International Policy Program. She is also a Senior Fellow (by courtesy) at the Hoover Institution.

event.description:
On our yearly theme: Micropower and the Non-human: Micropower, or the microphysics of power, is a category established by Foucault early on in his thinking, before his turn towards biopolitics. In Discipline and Punish (1975), Foucault posits that the microphysics of power’s “field of validity is situated in a sense between [state apparatuses] and the bodies themselves with their materiality and their forces.” (26). If, on the one hand, we understand bodies in an expanded sense, without privileging the human, and, on the other, we probe in de facto contemporary state apparatuses from the bottom up(algorithmic governance, corporate takeover of attention span, etc.), we find multiple opportunities to intervene. We would like to rekindle the spirit of the original formulation, revise Foucault, and set him into conversation with different archives, in keeping with the group’s orientation, Latin Americanist and otherwise.

On our yearly theme: Micropower and the Non-human: Micropower, or the microphysics of power, is a category established by Foucault early on in his thinking, before his turn towards biopolitics. 8:30 AM (PST) - 2:00 PM (PST) | 11:30 AM (EST) - 5:00 PM (EST)

event.title: E-IPER Dissertation Defense: Anaïs Voşki
event.description:
Please join us for an E-IPER dissertation defense by Anaïs Voşki: "From the ocean floor to outer space: Awe and the overview effect as pathways to pro-environmental psychological and behavioral change."

In-person: Y2E2 299

Virtual: Zoom webinar (passcode: 000000)

ABSTRACT

International consensus affirms that addressing the global environmental crisis requires transformative shifts in values and practices that center the fundamental interconnectedness between humans and nature, yet scalable psychological pathways toward such shifts remain elusive. Self-transcendent experiences—mental states characterized by reduced self-focus and increased connectedness beyond the self, such as awe, psychedelic, and peak experiences—offer one potential pathway. The overview effect, defined as the profound psychological shift reported by astronauts when viewing Earth from space, offers an exemplary case with both transformative potential and a distinctive pro-environmental profile. Beyond awe, many astronauts report transformed perceptions of Earth’s beauty, fragility, and value, as well as an enduring sense of ‘planetary interconnectedness,’ meaning a sense of being interlinked with the entire planet’s biosphere, including humanity and nature. Yet, within the rapidly closing window to meet global climate and biodiversity targets, only a fortunate few will ever view the Earth from space firsthand. This raises two related questions: Might virtual reality (VR) offer an opportunity to recreate the overview effect on Earth, and what might a phenomenologically faithful recreation require?

Across two randomized controlled experiments and a mixed methods systematic review, this dissertation addresses foundational gaps in overview effect research. It develops a systematic evidence base for how the overview effect is conceptualized and operationalized and tests the possibilities and limits of recreating it through VR. Chapter 1 provides the proof of concept for underwater VR as a means of amplifying pro-environmental emotional and behavioral responses, supporting its subsequent test in Chapter 3 as a microgravity analogue. Chapter 2 details findings of the systematic evidence synthesis, clarifying the phenomenon’s current conceptual and empirical boundaries. Chapter 3 extends the overview effect’s experimental operationalization beyond awe to include Earth perceptions and planetary interconnectedness, finding that underwater VR and a novel mindfulness-based attentional priming each amplified awe intensity without corresponding amplification in either Earth-related dimension. Together, these studies position Earth-based recreation of the overview effect as an unresolved question requiring both further conceptual clarification and a more rigorous evidence base. This research also provides a foundation for investigating how experiences with the potential for psychological transformation, such as the overview effect, may develop into enduring changes in how people perceive, relate to, and act toward the Earth.

event.title: CEE PhD Defense: Fletcher Passow, "Integrating Electric Truck Charging with the Electric Grid Under Electric Grid Capacity Constraints and Adoption Uncertainty"
event.description:
Abstract:

Freight trucks make up only a small fraction of U.S. vehicles but produce a large share of transportation greenhouse gas emissions. Adopting electric trucks would reduce emissions and local air pollution, but the high-power charging required would often demand upgrades to electric distribution grids near truck stops, warehouses, and factories — particularly to the substations that form the critical interface between distribution and transmission grids. These upgrade projects can take as much as 3-9 years and cost millions, while fleet operators can acquire electric trucks and build charging facilities in under a year. This timing asymmetry creates a structural bottleneck: fleet operators and charge point operators (CPOs) cannot confidently electrify without grid capacity, yet grid operators cannot confidently invest without evidence of charging demand. The result is a self-reinforcing deadlock. To contribute to breaking this deadlock, this dissertation explores ways that i) CPOs can reduce the grid capacity required for truck charging and ii) grid operators can plan ahead for charging in the face of substantial uncertainty about electric truck adoption.

event.title: Book Talk: Good Girls and Alpha Males: How Conservative Media is Targeting Gen Z
event.description:
Gen Z is coming of age in a world that feels stacked against them. That's exactly why conservative media is targeting them.

The fight for young minds is happening daily on podcasts, YouTube, and social media—platforms saturated with conservative messaging. The right has spent decades investing in this year-round digital propaganda apparatus, targeting Gen Z's economic insecurity and distrust of mainstream institutions to push answers rooted in hyper-individualism, misogyny, and bigotry.

In Good Girls and Alpha Males, journalist Madeline Peltz takes readers inside the online conservative sphere shaping the future of politics. From "tradwife" influencers to "manosphere" mouthpieces, she exposes the voices driving Gen Z's shift to the right along gendered lines. With equal ferocity, Peltz interrogates the Democratic Party's culpability, condemning the hostility to its younger, more progressive flank.

Personal and heartfelt, Good Girls and Alpha Males interweaves Peltz's own story with her coverage of right-wing media over the last decade. With deep empathy for a generation caught between disillusionment and radicalization, Peltz offers a wake-up call about the forces shaping Gen Z—and what the future holds if they go unchecked.

About the Author:

Madeline Peltz is a writer, journalist, and researcher born in Chicago. Over the last decade, her reporting has appeared in Media Matters for America, MSNOW, Newsweek, More Perfect Union, and more. She has been quoted as an expert on right-wing media and the conservative movement in the New York Times, CNN, Democracy Now!, the Washington Post, BBC, The Guardian, and elsewhere.

event.description:
Discover a new path into contemplative awareness by appreciating and participating in artistic expression during this interactive online class.

In this session, we will explore landscape drawings and paintings to experience the awe-inspiring relationships we share with the natural world and enhance our awareness of being part of something greater than ourselves. We’ll begin by setting intentions through viewing captivating landscapes and hearing inspiring words from writers, including Mary Oliver, Robert Frost, and others. event.title: Careers in International Law
event.description:
Join us for a career development workshop with Stanford scholars who will share practical advice on building a career in international law. Hear how they got started, what to look for in the field, and how to take your next steps.

This event is open to Stanford students only. RSVP is required, and lunch will be provided.

RSVP to attend

Panelists
E. Tendayi Achiume
Professor E. Tendayi Achiume is an international legal scholar focusing on international human rights law, international refugee law and international migration law. Her academic research explores the global governance of racism and xenophobia, and the legal and ethical implications of colonialism and other forms of empire for the governance of international migration. In recognition of the “exceptional creativity” and “promise for important future advances,” of Achiume’s research in these areas, she was awarded a 2023 MacArthur Fellowship, commonly known as the “genius grant”. She is also an Extraordinary Professor in the Department of Jurisprudence at the University of Pretoria; a Research Associate with the African Centre for Migration and Society at the University of Witwatersrand; and a Research Associate with the Refugee Studies Center at the University of Oxford. Professor Achiume will spend the 2024-2025 academic year as a scholar in residence at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton.

In November 2017, the United Nations Human Rights Council appointed Professor Achiume the UN Special Rapporteur on Contemporary Forms of Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance, making her the first woman to serve in this role since its creation in 1993. In 2016, she was appointed to co-chair the 2016 Annual Meeting of the American Society of International Law (ASIL), and she is former co-chair of the ASIL Migration Law Interest Group. In 2021, she was appointed to the American Journal of International Law Board of Editors and in 2022 selected as a commissioner for the O’Neill-Lancet Commission on Racism, Structural Discrimination and Global Health.

Before coming to Stanford Law, she was the inaugural Alicia Miñana Professor of Law at the UCLA School of Law, where she received the Distinguished Teaching Award in 2020, UCLA’s highest honor for excellence in teaching, as well as the Eby Award for the Art of Teaching. She also served as a faculty director of the UCLA Law Promise Institute for Human Rights.

She earned her B.A. from Yale University and her J.D. from Yale Law School. She also earned a Graduate Certificate in International Development Studies from Yale University, and an International Baccalaureate Diploma from the United World Colleges (UWC), Atlantic College.

Gulika Reddy
Gulika Reddy is a human rights advocate, and the Director of the International Human Rights and Conflict Resolution Clinic. Reddy has conducted human rights advocacy around the world, including in India, Kashmir, Yemen, the Central African Republic, and Papua New Guinea. Her work has focused on inequality, discrimination, armed conflict, peacebuilding, and the role of education in unlearning bias and fostering inclusion. Her academic research interests include critical perspectives on human rights, decolonial and anti-racist pedagogy, and the intersection between human rights and peacebuilding.

Most recently, Reddy was the Acting Director of the Human Rights Clinic and Co-Executive Director of the Human Rights Institute at Columbia Law School. Before joining Columbia Law School, Reddy worked with lawyers, non-profits, and academic institutions in India to prevent and respond to identity-based discrimination through litigation, legislative reform, grassroots activism, and public education. She is the Founder & Director of Schools of Equality, a non-profit organization in India that runs activity-based programs in schools with the aim to shift social attitudes that perpetuate gender-based violence and other forms of identity-based discrimination.

Reddy received an MPP from Harvard Kennedy School of Government, where she was a Dubin Leadership Fellow, and an LL.M. from Columbia Law School, where she was a Human Rights Fellow. In 2016, Columbia Law School’s Human Rights Institute awarded her a Commendation for Leadership and Commitment in Human Rights, the World Economic Forum named her one of the Davos 50, and she was invited to attend their 2016 Annual Meeting in Davos. Reddy was also awarded the TalentNomics Global Emerging Game-Changer award for exemplary dedication to the empowerment of women and girls.

Moderator
Penelope Van Tuyl
Penelope Van Tuyl is a human rights lawyer who has worked closely with founding Director, David Cohen, for nearly two decades to shape Stanford's Center for Human Rights and International Justice into the vibrant academic and research community it is today. She first joined (what was then known as the Berkeley War Crimes Studies Center) in 2006 as a trial monitor working in Sierra Leone and Cambodia, and was hired full time in 2008 to oversee several key initiatives in Southeast Asia, West Africa, Europe, and the United States. She was promoted to Associate Director in 2011, and shepherded the Center through its 2013 transition from Berkeley to Stanford, which spurred a exciting period of rapid programatic growth. As Associate Director, Van Tuyl is integrally involved with all aspects of the Center's administration and strategic planning across program areas, on campus and overseas. She serves in a principal leadership position, managing the Center's digital archival partnership withe the Stanford University Libraries. She also runs the Minor in Human Rights, and teaches the required core course for the Minor HUMRTS 101: Cross-Disciplinary Perspectives on Human Rights Theory and Practice. Of the many hats she wears in her job, however, her favorite is that of mentor and advisor to the wonderful Stanford students who pass through the Center.

Van Tuyl has authored and edited numerous reports and articles on international criminal law and procedure. Her research interests touch on substantive, procedural, and administrative aspects of international criminal law practice, including Joint Criminal Enterprise liability, standards of pleading in international courts, and the institutional accountability mechanisms that are meant to support the effective and efficient administration of justice. She also writes and teaches about migration and asylum law in comparative perspective. Van Tuyl graduated Summa Cum Laude from Amherst College, with a BA in International Relations and Latin American Studies. She received her J.D. from the University of California, Berkeley School of Law, and is admitted to practice in the state of California.
